# Judge J3 — RL data lens: Daliesk Village

Reviewing: `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-deepseek-harness/f53f80cc-1f77-5d02-a862-99d59ffabdce/scratchpad/daliesk-village-design.md` (v1, 2026-09-05).
Lens: DeepSeek-style RLVR, GRPO grouping, environment-first pipelines, decontamination, and the training-data value of a corpus like the AI Village HuggingFace dataset.

No `ai-village-dossier.md` existed in the scratchpad directory at review time; AI Village facts below come from a fetch of `https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village` and `https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025`, each summarized by a fetch-time model rather than read as raw text — flagged wherever precision matters (section 4).

## 1. Verdict: 6/10, and the marginal-cost estimate the question asks for

**The comparison as posed is partly a category error.** The design's own mapping table places the actual RLVR data mechanism inside the Proving Ground district: "the environment suite, training-eligible and held-out, run as fleet cells by every model route we license, with pass@k per policy version" (`daliesk-village-design.md`, "Three districts, one log"). That is the identical mechanism `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md` (W3) already specifies for goal 3: "The unit of data is a group of rollouts of one environment under one policy version, produced on demand by the runner." Running that mechanism on an always-on public shift schedule versus a scheduled offline batch job changes *when and how visibly* the groups are produced, not what a group is. So "always-on" is an operations wrapper around environment-first generation, not a competing data-generation mechanism, and the note's own Alternatives Considered section is explicit that the *other* candidate mechanism — harvesting persistent, open-ended fleet sessions directly, i.e., an AI-Village-shaped format — was tried and rejected: "a fleet session carries no environment identity, no group, and no seed, so decontamination, curriculum sampling, and GRPO grouping had nothing to key on. This is rejected in favor of an environment-first, group-first factory" (`four-goal-workflows.md`, Alternatives Considered, "Fleet sessions as reinforcement-learning data").

**What the always-on wrapper genuinely adds**, none of it a different RL mechanism: (a) a continuous feed of new environment candidates mined from real client failures rather than a one-off authoring effort — W3 stage 1's `EnvironmentProposal` is produced by the "Environment Synthesizer" from "failures, client checks," and Workshop (W2) is the only district that generates those; (b) continuous recalibration (`EnvironmentStats.pass1`/`pass8`) as harness variants and policy versions change, because the fleet never stops running; (c) a public, comparably-measured leaderboard, which is a legitimacy and decontamination-discipline forcing function, not a data quality improvement per se; (d) a standing supply of certified trajectories for the W3 stage 4 SFT cold start. These are real and worth the always-on framing.

**What it does not add**, and what it puts at risk: it adds nothing to GRPO group validity itself (that is entirely a runner and stamp question, answered in section 5), and it introduces two costs specific to being always-on and public that an offline batch pipeline does not carry: (i) resource contention between fleet-serving compute and RL-training compute on the same hardware (see gap 5, section 3), most acute exactly under Scenario A's two fixed devices; (ii) reputational and decontamination exposure from publishing a live observatory before the defenses that make a certificate trustworthy are complete (see the answer to open question 3). The design doc's own "Risks the Village makes concrete" section already names the public-failure and cost-of-always-on risks; it does not name the GPU-contention risk.

**Score: 6/10.** Worth building, net positive specifically as an environment-mining, calibration, and cold-start engine layered on top of the environment-first mechanism the harness already commits to — but the premise that always-on operation *itself* makes the RL data better is not supported by the documents; the actual mechanism is unchanged, several of its current gaps (section 3) make even the offline-alone version not yet GRPO-clean, and the always-on framing adds real unaddressed operational risk that an offline batch pipeline would not.

**Marginal cost per certified trajectory.** The harness cannot compute this figure from the log today: `packages/improvement/scorekeeper/README.md`, Known Limitations, states plainly "Cost is not a field — pricing lives in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy`'s configuration rather than in the log, so a facts record states tokens and names a breached cap but never a EUR amount." The design doc's claim that "the scorekeeper reports cost per certified session per route" (`daliesk-village-design.md`, "Budgets") is therefore not yet true of the shipped package; and `EvalReport.costPerCertified`, named as a W3 stage-6 hand-off field in `four-goal-workflows.md`, has no producer yet either. What follows is a judge's engineering estimate under stated assumptions, not a harness-sourced fact:

Formula: marginal €/certified trajectory ≈ (compute cost per rollout) ÷ (certificate rate), where certificate rate is the scorekeeper's `certified / runs` (`scorekeeper/README.md`, "Scoreboard rows"). Certificate rate, not €/token, is the dominant lever in both scenarios below — a 20% versus 60% pass rate is a 3x change in this number for identical hardware.

- **Scenario A — two DGX Spark plus cloud.** Using NVIDIA's own published specifications for DGX Spark as general hardware knowledge (not a document read for this review): 128GB unified memory and roughly one petaflop of FP4-sparse compute per unit, list price on the order of $4,000 each, with two units linkable for larger single-model serving. A ~120B open-weight MoE model at 4-bit quantization fits in one unit's memory with headroom for KV cache. Capital amortized over an 18-month hardware cycle is roughly $0.62/hour for the pair; electricity at typical desktop-class draw is a few cents per hour. At that scale the self-hosted, open-weight portion of the fleet is throughput-bound, not dollar-bound: assuming an illustrative 150–400 output tok/s aggregate across both units and a 5,000-token rollout, hardware-plus-power cost per certified trajectory at a 20–60% certificate rate lands in the range of a few euro-cents to roughly €0.50. The number that is not near-zero is cloud burst for the licensed frontier comparison routes (closed-weight, billed at published API rates, order €0.5–5 per million tokens) and any rollout overflow beyond the two units' throughput; that spend scales with how much frontier-route comparison volume the shift runs, which the design doc does not bound separately from the open-weight fleet's cell budget.
- **Scenario B — 500k€ of on-prem GPUs.** Illustrative build: roughly 12–16 H100/H200-class cards after non-GPU capex (networking, storage, hosting), enough concurrent high-bandwidth memory to hold the RL trainer, a frozen reference copy, and multiple rollout replicas of a 120B model at once — the first of the two scenarios that can run the actual GRPO gradient step in-house rather than inference/calibration only. Amortized over three years, compute-only capex is roughly €19/hour for the whole cluster; all-in with power, cooling, and hosting overhead, call it €25–30/hour. At an illustrative 2,000–8,000 output tok/s aggregate, marginal €/certified trajectory at a 20–60% certificate rate is on the order of €0.02–0.15 — lower than Scenario A per trajectory, but the same GPUs must be shared across fleet-serving, the trainer, and held-out evaluation (gap 5), so realized per-activity throughput is lower than this theoretical aggregate once contention is accounted for, and the €25–30/hour is sunk whether or not the fleet is actually saturated.

Both estimates should be treated as order-of-magnitude only; neither scenario's real number can be produced until cost is a logged, foldable field (gap 3) rather than a config value joined out of band.

## 2. The four open questions

**Q1 — show frontier routes by name from day one, or only after a paired experiment (same preset, same isolation)?**
Only after a paired experiment. `LeaderboardRow` (implemented, per `four-goal-workflows.md` W1 stage 3 prose) "never averages across `isolation` or `heldOut`," and `EvalReport` "pins the harness variant hash it ran under, and an evaluation on an unpinned variant is rejected as not comparable" (W3 stage 6 acceptance criterion). An unpaired, differently-isolated named comparison published before those disciplines apply reproduces exactly the failure mode the AI Village's own retrospective names as its top self-identified limitation — "existence proofs, not controlled experiments" (`https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025`, "Stated Methodology Limitations") — while looking, to a public reader, like a controlled one. It also creates a public artifact whose provenance (preset, isolation) is not matched across routes, which is the same information a later decontamination or audit pass would need and would not have if the comparison predates a frozen `ExperimentPlan` digest.

**Q2 — is a weekly cadence right for a factory district whose goals are client deliveries with their own deadlines?**
No, and the design doc's own "Goal cadence" bullet does not scope the weekly cadence to the district it fits. Weekly, frozen `SuitePlan`s belong to Proving Ground (W1 stage 2, W3 stage 2) and, for its own keep-or-retire and nomination rhythm, to Commons (W4 stages 5–6) — neither carries an external deadline. Workshop goals are tracked by `ProgramLedger` events "mapping every goal of a program to its session, workspace, preset, isolation, budget, and status" with a `Plan` "derived from the compiled standards rather than authored freely beforehand" (`four-goal-workflows.md`, W2 stage 5) — that ledger, not a weekly boundary, is what should pace Workshop. Forcing Workshop onto the Proving Ground's cadence throttles the one district that feeds the W3 stage 1 environment factory ("failures, client checks" → `EnvironmentProposal`) to a weekly batch instead of an event-driven stream keyed on each goal's own `IntegrationReport`/`ReleaseRecord` closing, which degrades curriculum freshness (W4 stage 10 `CurriculumUpdate`) for no benefit to client delivery.

**Q3 — do slices 1–4 of the read barrier plus budget policy make the first shift honest, or does tamper (6) have to land first?**
Tamper detection (slice 6) has to land first for any certificate rate that will be trusted as an RL reward signal or a public capability number; slices 1–4 alone are not enough. The three defenses cover different attack surfaces, per `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-read-barrier.md`: slices 1–4 (landed) stop the implementer from *reading* the standard ("a command line the implementer can observe in a process listing names a file whose content it cannot read," line 23); slice 5 (pending) closes the same read-prevention hole across every capability seam beyond the filesystem — "`deniedReadRoots` on `SandboxPolicy`... This is the slice that makes `process` claimable" (line 122); slice 6 (pending) is the only one that stops the implementer from *writing* to check-owned paths undetected — it adds a baseline-versus-per-attempt digest over `EnvironmentDefinition.task.immutable` paths and a `verdict: 'pass' | 'fail' | 'tampered'` on `verification/run`, where "a digest that differs from the baseline is `tampered`... and never calls `recordRun`, so no certificate can exist for that run" (line 73). `four-goal-workflows.md`'s own Alternatives Considered names exactly this class of exploit as the fast one: reward computed in the implementer's own workspace is rejected because "editing tests, `conftest.py`, or a package script earns a certificate — and reinforcement learning finds this exploit within tens of steps." Slices 1–4 defend against *knowing the answer*; slice 6 defends against *rewriting the answer key*, which is the more dangerous gap once GRPO is actually optimizing against the signal, because it corrupts the reward itself rather than merely leaking information. Until slice 6 lands, the first shift's certificate rate is at most a Workshop/human-reviewed diff signal (W2 already has a human reviewer at stage 9 as a second check) — never a number fed to W3 stage 5 or published unqualified as a capability leaderboard. Whatever isolation the first shift actually runs under must also be disclosed and never blended, per the note's own risk: "Under `isolation: none`, checks run with the implementer's privileges in the implementer's own workspace, so a certificate there is not evidence a client or a trainer should treat as strong; leaderboards and training exports must partition by isolation, never blend it" (`four-goal-workflows.md`, Risks, "Cheap reward under weak isolation").

**Q4 — which base-model routes run the proving ground first, given scenarios A and B?**
No specific base route is named anywhere in this repository — a search of `packages/` and `.agents/notes/` for a pinned target model or roster returns nothing beyond the note's own "roughly 120B-parameter" phrasing. The right answer is therefore a selection rule the `CapabilityMatrix` (W1 stage 1) should encode from config, not a name fixed by this review: prioritize open-weight routes whose native or quantized memory footprint fits the scenario's hardware without cloud offload for inference (so calibration and cold-start rollouts are cheap), whose licence permits training on derived outputs, and whose parameter class is close enough to the ~120B target that `EnvironmentStats` difficulty and curriculum data transfer. Under Scenario A, that selects routes servable within a single DGX Spark's 128GB at 4-bit-class quantization — as of this review, an openly-licensed ~120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model designed for exactly that memory envelope (illustrative fit, not a repository commitment) is the kind of candidate that belongs in the first `CapabilityMatrix` cell; larger or denser open-weight candidates in the same class should wait for Scenario B, where the on-prem cluster (section 1) has the concurrent high-bandwidth memory to also run the RL trainer rather than inference alone. Licensed frontier routes should enter only as the fixed comparison arm of a paired `ExperimentPlan`, never as a proving-ground base-model candidate, consistent with "Roster... Open-weight routes first (the base-model candidates for goal 3), the licensed frontier routes second" (`daliesk-village-design.md`, "The design").

## 4. The AI Village dataset in Daliesk's work

**What the licence states**, per the dataset page (`https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village`, summarized by a fetch-time model, not read verbatim — a data steward should confirm the exact clause text before any use is finalized): a custom licence named "ai-village-research-terms" that requires the accepting user to (a) not train or fine-tune AI systems on the dataset **without AI Digest's written permission** — a permission-gated restriction, not an unconditional ban; (b) not attempt to re-identify individuals appearing in it; (c) cite AI Digest / AI Village in any resulting publication; (d) notify the creators about resulting work. The dataset totals 176GB, ~1.14M computer-use turns, ~123k chat messages, ~165k memories, ~37k sessions, refreshed roughly weekly; screenshots are referenced rather than inlined. These figures match the design doc's "1.14M computer-use turns, 123k chat messages, 165k memories, 37k sessions" (`daliesk-village-design.md`, "What the AI Village is").

**As training data: excluded**, absent written permission. This maps directly onto a schema the harness already has: `DataUseTerms.purposes[]` is `delivery` / `training` / `evaluation` (`four-goal-workflows.md`, Structured hand-offs). Any session or artifact derived from this dataset should carry `purposes: [evaluation]` only, never `training`, and the curator's `DatasetManifest.consentScope` (W3 stage 3) should name the exclusion explicitly rather than relying on the dataset simply never being mounted where an exporter can reach it — the design doc's own risk list already calls for exactly this discipline elsewhere ("A sample whose consent scope is unknown is dropped, never assumed," W3 stage 3 On-failure column).

**As evaluation: permitted in intent, not addressed in the fetched terms.** The licence is framed as a research licence and the dataset's stated purpose is "studying agentic behaviour, multi-agent dynamics, long-horizon memory, human–agent interaction" — consistent with reading it to inform evaluation design — but the fetched summary enumerates only prohibitions and obligations, not an affirmative evaluation grant; a data steward should confirm this reading against the actual terms page rather than this review's paraphrase.

**As behaviour taxonomy: the strongest, lowest-risk fit.** The corpus's documented failure classes — deception without intent (64 fabrication-intent cases found across 109,000 reasoning summaries, per `https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025`), sycophantic spread of a teammate's hallucination, metric gaming via an external tool (Stockfish in a chess goal), goal abandonment, and catastrophizing — are a direct checklist for extending `SessionDiagnosis.taxonomy` (currently `tool-misuse` / `context-loss` / `spec-misread` / `verification-gaming` / `loop` / `environment-defect` / `model-limit`, `four-goal-workflows.md`, Structured hand-offs) or for authoring `hiddenChecks` that specifically test for each class. Reading a public retrospective to extend a taxonomy is analysis, not training, and stays clearly inside a research licence's intent.

**As environment mining: the second-strongest fit, with one hard constraint.** Authoring new `EnvironmentDefinition`s whose `hiddenChecks` target these exact failure classes (e.g., an outreach environment that fails a check if a claim about a contacted third party is asserted without verification, mirroring the ~300 fabricated-NGO-partnership emails the retrospective reports) is legitimate research use and produces environments nobody else's harness has, because nobody else has run an always-on multi-agent village at this scale. The hard constraint is the licence's re-identification clause: the retrospective reports emails sent mostly to nonexistent addresses but some real ones, so no environment authored from this material may embed a verbatim transcript excerpt, a real name, or a real address — every mined environment must be resynthesized with invented entities, never copied forward, both because copying is a redistribution and re-identification risk and because `EnvironmentProposal.sourceSessions[]` (`SessionId`, `four-goal-workflows.md`) is typed to Daliesk's own branded session ids and has no field for an external corpus's session identifiers.

**Net recommendation:** mount it, if at all, only under a `DataUseTerms` record scoped to `evaluation`, never `training`, feed it into the taxonomy and environment-mining paths above with full resynthesis of any concrete entity, cite and notify per the licence's stated obligations, and have the accountable data-steward role (`SignoffRecord.role: data-steward`, already named in the note) read the actual terms page before the first use — not this review's summary of a fetch.

## 5. Exact stamp, group, and repetition fields for GRPO grouping and decontamination from the log alone

The `environment/run` event the environment runner appends before a run's first turn (`EnvironmentRunStamp`, implemented, per `four-goal-workflows.md`) carries, today:

- `environmentId` (`EnvironmentId`)
- `environmentKind` (string)
- `heldOut` (boolean — export drops the line unless asked to keep it, per `trajectories/README.md`)
- `promptSha256` (hex)
- `checksSha256` (hex)
- `fixtureSha256?` (hex, absent for a task with no fixture)
- `contentSha256` (hex over the three hashes above — "the decontamination key")
- `repetition` (int, zero-based, the group-sampling index)
- `group?` (string, batch identity)
- `model` (`{provider, model}`)
- `isolation` (`CertificateIsolation`)

**Decontamination works from the log alone today.** `contentSha256` plus `heldOut` is sufficient for exact-match decontamination and export withholding: the trajectory exporter already withholds any session "whose `environment/run` stamp marks a held-out environment... unless `includeHeldOut: true`" (`trajectories/README.md`), and P6 states this hash is what "decontamination and export withholding key on" (`four-goal-workflows.md`). This does not cover near-duplicate contamination (a reworded but substantively identical task); see gap 4.

**GRPO grouping does not yet work from the log alone.** `group` and `repetition` correctly identify which rollouts belong to one batch and a rollout's position within it, but GRPO's advantage computation is only valid if every rollout in a `group` also shares one policy checkpoint — and `model: {provider, model}` names a route, not a checkpoint or training step, so two rollouts in the same `group` could in principle have been produced by different points of an in-training policy with nothing in the log to catch it. The two fields that close this gap — `policyVersion` and `seed` — are both named in the note as "proposed extensions this event does not yet carry" (same field list) and are independently confirmed missing by `experiments/README.md`'s own limitation ("the `environment/run` stamp carries no seed, so pairing removes environment variance but not run-to-run variance") and by the note's aspirational `SessionFacts` schema, which already lists `seed`, `policy_version`, `group_id`, `rollout_index`, `environment_content_hash`, `fixture_sha256`, and `checks_sha256` as council-added identity fields (`four-goal-workflows.md`, "Scoreboard row," line 209) that have no producing event yet. `seed` and `policyVersion` serve two distinct purposes and should not be conflated: `policyVersion` is what makes a claimed GRPO group admissible at all (every member must match); `seed` is what the experiment service needs for paired variance reduction across arms and for exact rollout reproducibility, not for the GRPO math itself, since GRPO wants stochastic diversity within a group rather than a shared seed across its members.

**Minimum field set a shift must carry, once gap 1 lands:** `environmentId`, `contentSha256`, `group`, `repetition`, `policyVersion`, and `isolation` together let a consumer partition the log into GRPO-admissible groups (same `environmentId` + `contentSha256` + `group` + `policyVersion`, ordered by `repetition`) and decontaminate against the held-out suite (`contentSha256` + `heldOut`) without joining anything outside the session log; `seed` and `model` remain necessary for reproducibility and route attribution but are not load-bearing for either GRPO validity or decontamination itself.
